newsitem.title: USA: Clinton has little time to enjoy re-election.
newsitem.headline: Clinton has little time to enjoy re-election.

text.p: President Bill Clinton grappled with top level Cabinet resignations and pleaded with Republicans to work with him -- not against him -- as he returned to Washington on Wednesday to savor his re-election triumph.

Hundreds of White House workers and Democratic party officals gave him a hero's welcome on the south lawn of the White House. They wore T-shirts with pictures of the presidential mansion, saying "Welcome Home."

The 50-year-old Clinton, whose rocky start in the White House led many to believe he would be a one-term president, told them: "Two years ago not many people believed we would be here. But I believed if we just kept doing the right things, kept trying to do them in the right way and kept working hard ... the American people would render the right judgment."

As Clinton flew back to Washington for the White House celebration, officials said Secretary of State Warren Christopher, Defence Secretary William Perry and Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor had given notice they would leave his Cabinet. Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary confirmed she also would resign.

The resignations were just the start of what is expected to be a wholesale departure of top aides, including possibly Attorney General Janet Reno, White House Chief of Staff Leon Panetta and close adviser George Stephanopoulos.

Clinton is under pressure to try to to reach out to Republicans, who kept control of Congress, to fill some of the gaps -- with many advising him to choose Indiana Sen. Richard Lugar, former Maine Sen. William Cohen or retired general Colin Powell for a top spot.
Many would also like to see him appoint his defeated Republican rival, Bob Dole, to a position -- perhaps as head of a commission to review how to save Medicare or Social Security entitlements.
Fully aware he had won only a partial triumph because Republicans held control of the House of Representatives and the Senate, Clinton pleaded for cooperation not confrontation.

He told reporters, "If we can recreate for the next four years the spirit that existed in Congress in the last six weeks (of the last term, when a number of compromise bills were approved) we can do great things."

Voters gave Clinton only a partial triumph. They re-elected him by a margin of 49 percent to 41 percent for Republican rival Bob Dole, but allowed the Republicans to call the shots in both houses of Congress -- a move that many predict will lead not to cooperation but to cut-throat political infighting and give-no-quarter investigations of White House scandals.
"How can a Republican Congress work with a man it wants to indict," was one question thrown at Republican Party Chairman Haley Barbour at a National Press Club luncheon.

Barbour tried to play down the Republican differences with Clinton, saying Congress doesn't indict anyone. But Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi said the newly-elected Congress will hold hearings on the Democrats' campaign finances.
"I'm sure we'll have some hearings," Lott said of the scandal that involved raising millions of dollars in contributions from an Indonesian conglomerate and other foreign businesses.

The proposed Senate hearings would be in addition to a multitude of congressional hearings that have already been held and three investigations underway by independent counsels probing Clinton, his wife, his aides and associates.

For Clinton, the list of still unresolved issues seems endless -- from the Whitewater land deal he and his wife Hillary invested in years ago to questions about possible obstruction of justice by people in his White House.

The New York Times said on Wednesday that Clinton must clean house if necessary and cooperate with legitimate inquiries "if he wants to avoid being remembered simply as the most investigated president in the modern era."
The sudden flurry of departure disclosures served to dissipate some of the post-election euphoria and to underscore the heavy decisions that lie ahead for the president.

The Republicans increased their majority in the Senate by at least one from the previous 53-47 majority. They had won 54 seats to the Democrats' 45 with one seat in Oregon still too close to call. Projections said they would retain a slight majority in the House of Representatives once a number of undecided races were settled.

While White House aides tried to play up Clinton's victory over Dole as impressive enough to amount to a symbolic mandate, his numbers were solid but relatively modest by comparison with other recent presidents.

Official returns with more than 99 percent of voting precincts counted showed he had won 49.2 percent of the popular support to 40.8 percent for Dole and 8.5 percent for Reform Party candidate Ross Perot.

While Clinton became the first Democratic president to win re-election since Franklin Roosevelt in 1944, he also became the first president of either party to be re-elected without majority support in 80 years, since Woodrow Wilson in 1916.
